description:
We are BigHero_6 – six young minds united by one ambition: to make a difference! Inspired by the animated movie, “Big” represents bold ideas, “Hero” embodies innovation, and “6” symbolizes our unity.
Passionate about science, AI, coding, and space technology, our project “Harmonizing MODIS and VIIRS Hotspots” aims to combine satellite data to improve hotspot monitoring, support wildfire early warning, and protect the environment.
BigHero_6 – Think Big, Act Bold, Make an Impact!

It provides matching land filters across views, two 12-hour observation counts, next-step guidance and notices of newly received records while the page is open. A frozen seven-day study in northern Australia groups observations into common cells and UTC dates, fits count scaling on earlier dates and evaluates it on later dates. This improves agreement with MODIS counts within the selected test sample. The prototype makes observations easier to inspect while preserving acquisition times and limitations. It does not measure land temperature, confirm ground fires or predict spread. Longer records, coverage information, user research and independent validation remain necessary.
details:
FireWatch is a project developed by team BIGHERO_6 to address two connected challenges in wildfire monitoring: residents and land managers often find it difficult to interpret satellite hotspot information near their areas of interest, while MODIS and VIIRS observations differ in spatial resolution and sampling frequency, making their data difficult to compare and combine.

The project introduces a bilingual web platform powered by real NASA FIRMS data. Users can search for locations, save areas of interest, select monitoring radii of 5 km, 10 km, or 20 km, and explore nearby satellite detections on an interactive map. The platform supports consistent land and time filters across different views, displays observation counts across two consecutive 12-hour periods, and provides notices when new records are received while the page remains open. These features make satellite observations more accessible and easier to explore.

Alongside the web prototype, the team conducted a seven-day study in northern Australia from November 6 to 12, 2026. MODIS and VIIRS observations were grouped into a common 0.25-degree grid and UTC dates. A scaling factor was fitted using earlier dates and evaluated on later dates. Through-origin least squares using 211 paired-positive cell-days in the training set produced an alpha value of 0.158777904605. On 162 held-out cell-days, MAE decreased from 12.851852 to 2.983652, while RMSE decreased from 22.049047 to 4.457109, measured in MODIS records per selected cell-day. These results demonstrate improved count agreement within the selected test sample, but do not establish field accuracy or global transferability.

The project uses React, TypeScript, Leaflet, and React Leaflet to build its interactive mapping interface, with Vite and Vinext supporting development and deployment. Cloudflare Workers handles data retrieval, geocoding, and access authorization. Satellite observations come from NASA FIRMS, including MODIS Terra/Aqua C6.1 NRT and NOAA-20 VIIRS C2 NRT. OpenStreetMap provides map data, while Photon supports location search.

FireWatch's innovation lies in combining a practical satellite-data visualization and monitoring tool with a scientific workflow for harmonizing observations from two different satellite systems. Instead of simply displaying raw data, the team developed a method to organize observations into common spatial and temporal units, enabling more consistent comparisons. The project also preserves acquisition times and clearly communicates the limitations of its results.
Throughout development, the team considered differences in MODIS and VIIRS spatial resolution and sampling frequency, spatial and temporal consistency in data comparison, source reliability, user experience, and research reproducibility. The team also recognized that satellite hotspots are thermal anomaly observations, not confirmed ground fires; record counts do not represent land-surface temperature or verified fire incidents. FireWatch does not predict fire spread. Longer observation records, coverage information, user research, and independent evaluations are still needed for further development.
